title: Cost drift analysis notes (GPU spend vs token-attributed cost) — WIP
body:
Context / why this doc exists
- We keep seeing mismatches between (A) observed GPU spend (cloud billing + internal allocator) and (B) token-attributed “standard cost” numbers computed from telemetry primitives.
- This is blocking:
  - Finance confidence in unit economics rollups (monthly windows)
  - Console cost breakdown credibility (customer questions + support tickets)
  - Optimize ROI estimates (what-if savings must not exceed reality)
- This is not a single bug; it looks like a combination of measurement gaps + policy choices (overhead allocation) + timing windows.

Scope for this analysis (current)
- Regions: us-east-1, eu-west-1 (hosted) + 2 dedicated clusters (customers redacted)
- Time windows tested: 2026-01-20 → 2026-02-18 (daily)
- Models: top 5 by token volume (mix of 7B/13B/34B) + 1 embeddings model
- Primary comparison: daily spend vs daily predicted cost totals (by deployment_mode + cluster)

Definitions (for sanity)
A) “Observed GPU spend” (ground-ish truth)
- Cloud line items + amortized reserved instances, mapped to cluster using tags
- Includes idle / fragmentation / headroom unless explicitly removed
- Includes non-request GPU time (warmup, health checks, canaries, failed jobs) unless removed

B) “Token-attributed cost” (what we compute)
- Sum over requests of request_attributable_cost (prefill + decode) + allocated_overhead where applicable
- Driven by:
  - token metering (prefill_tokens, decode_tokens)
  - runtime efficiency modifiers (batch efficiency, cache hit rate)
  - model/runtime metadata (quant profile, kernels, hw SKU)
  - policy: overhead allocation (what’s counted + how it’s apportioned)

Current drift metric proposal (draft)
- Drift% = (predicted_total_cost - observed_spend_mapped) / observed_spend_mapped
- Also tracking absolute error per day and rolling 7d mean.
- NOTE: If policy excludes some spend from the predicted numerator, drift is expected; needs explicit decomposition.

Quick summary of what we’re seeing (as of 2026-02-18)
- Hosted clusters:
  - Daily drift ranges: -18% to +9% depending on region/day
  - Strong correlation with traffic spikes + telemetry lag incidents
- Dedicated clusters:
  - Drift often negative (predicted < observed) by 10–25%
  - Looks dominated by idle/headroom + customer-specific autoscaling config
- Biggest single-day outlier: 2026-02-11 us-east-1 predicted +14% (later traced to telemetry backfill + double-counted decode tokens during prefill/decode split bug)

High-level breakdown attempt
We tried decomposing spend and predicted totals into buckets.

Observed spend decomposition (what we can compute today)
- GPU compute (allocated to serving nodes)
- GPU idle/headroom (estimated: provisioned - utilized)
- Non-request GPU time (warmup/health checks)
- “Unknown / untagged” (billing items missing cluster tags)

Predicted cost decomposition (what standard cost model intends)
- Request-attributable
  - Prefill
  - Decode
  - KV cache effects (reduced prefill work, sometimes increased memory pressure)
  - Batching efficiency (throughput improvements)
- Overhead allocation
  - Control plane overhead
  - Headroom reserve (policy-dependent)
  - “Platform tax” (SRE/ops, etc.) — finance-defined but must be transparent

Key observation: policy mismatch is a major source of apparent drift
- Finance mapping includes headroom and some idle as real spend (because it is).
- Current token-attributed cost often excludes headroom/idle unless “allocated_overhead” is enabled and configured.
- Conclusion: drift must be measured in two modes:
  1) “Request-attributable drift” (compare only spend that is reasonably request-driven)
  2) “All-in drift” (include overhead allocation policy to match full spend)

Data sources & joins (pain points)
- Billing/allocator:
  - Daily spend by cluster_id + gpu_sku + region
  - Known gap: ~1–3% of spend lacks correct tags for ephemeral nodes
- Telemetry:
  - Request metering (token counts; prefill/decode split)
  - Runtime metrics: batch_size, batch_efficiency, queue_time, kv_cache_hits/misses
  - Known gap: runtime metric export has inconsistent dimensions across versions
- Model catalog:
  - model_id -> hw_sku compatibility, quant_profile_id
  - Known gap: quant profile IDs were not stable historically (ENG-4829 / PR-28502 addresses)

Hypotheses for drift (ranked by likelihood / impact)
H1) Telemetry lag + late-arriving events shift tokens into wrong day
- Symptom: daily predicted totals “jump” after backfill; spend is stable.
- Example: 2026-02-14 eu-west-1 saw predicted +7% on rerun after ingest caught up.
- What to do:
  - For dashboards: always compute with a watermark (e.g., T-6h or T-24h) and show “data freshness”.
  - For finance: run monthly close jobs using fixed watermarks and backfill rules.

H2) Prefill/decode split bug / version skew in runtime exporters
- Symptom: double-counting decode tokens for some runtime versions (reported in runtime thread; fixed later).
- Action:
  - Add conformance tests: prefill_tokens + decode_tokens must equal total_tokens across sampled requests.
  - Track schema_version distribution and correlate with drift spikes.

H3) Incorrect batching efficiency interpretation (units mismatch)
- Symptom: predicted compute cost too low when batch_efficiency is treated as multiplier vs divisor.
- Current confusion: is batch_efficiency defined as “effective tokens/sec relative to baseline (>=1)” or “wasted fraction (0..1)”? Some pipelines emit both.
- Action:
  - Lock semantics in cost spec; reject ambiguous values in API.
  - Add metric name normalization + explicit units (ENG-4823).

H4) KV cache accounting doesn’t reflect memory pressure / eviction behavior
- Symptom: predicted savings from cache hits, but observed spend doesn’t drop (or drops less).
- Possible reasons:
  - Cache increases memory footprint causing lower effective concurrency.
  - Evictions cause cache hit rate to look ok but don’t translate to compute savings.
- Action:
  - Need runtime-exported cache residency/eviction stats (ENG-4828). Today we mostly have hit rate.

H5) GPU utilization baseline is wrong (allocator sees high idle; predicted assumes perfect packing)
- Symptom: dedicated clusters negative drift consistently.
- Likely real: customers pay for reserved headroom + isolation; token-attributed costs shouldn’t pretend this isn’t spend.
- Action:
  - Explicit overhead allocation mode for Dedicated: allocate idle/headroom by customer policy (e.g., per-reserved-capacity-hour + variable per-token).

H6) Quantization profile not applied / mixed execution paths
- Symptom: predicted cost off by model/version transitions; quant kernels differ from catalog metadata.
- Action:
  - Ensure runtime emits execution_path_id and quant_profile_id used (not only “requested”).
  - Validate catalog mapping weekly.

What we tried (notes from experiments)
Experiment 1: Remove “unknown/untagged” spend
- Method: filter billing items without cluster_id tags
- Result: drift improved by ~1–2% absolute in hosted, negligible in dedicated
- Takeaway: helps but not the main issue.

Experiment 2: Apply a simple daily watermark (ignore last 12h of telemetry)
- Method: compute predicted totals only for requests with event_time <= now-12h
- Result: reduced day-to-day volatility; drift band narrowed by ~3–5% for hosted
- Tradeoff: Console dashboards “lag” but become more trustworthy.

Experiment 3: Compare “request-attributable only” vs “all-in”
- Method: observed spend split into estimated request-driven spend (utilized GPU time) and overhead (idle/headroom)
- Result:
  - Request-attributable drift is much tighter (typically within ±5% when telemetry is fresh)
  - All-in drift remains negative for dedicated unless we allocate overhead
- Takeaway: we need two numbers and we must label them clearly.

Open questions (need decisions / inputs)
1) What is the canonical overhead allocation policy in v1?
- Laura/Rishi thread suggests making overhead explicit and reported separately, with a default allocation method for finance windows.
- We need to know:
  - Do we allocate headroom proportionally by tokens? by reserved capacity? by peak concurrency? mixture?
  - What do we do for multi-tenant hosted where idle is shared across many workloads?

2) What is “observed spend mapped” in the presence of reserved instances and preemptible?
- Need an allocator “bill of materials” doc we can reference.

3) How to treat retries and failed requests?
- Telemetry includes attempts; billing might include the GPU time even if request failed.
- Console wants customer-visible breakdown; do we show failed request cost separately?

Data quality gaps (concrete)
- Missing/unstable dimensions:
  - runtime version and execution_path_id not always present in request logs
  - kv_cache eviction/residency metrics absent
  - batch efficiency semantics inconsistent across exporters
- Join keys:
  - request_id not stable across some proxy layers (hosted)
  - cluster_id tagging missing for ephemeral nodes (billing)
- Timing:
  - event_time vs ingest_time confusion in a few pipelines; some backfills rewrite event_time

Recommendations (near-term)
1) Implement drift SLI with watermarking + “freshness” indicator
- SLI should be computed on a stable window (e.g., T-24h) to avoid chasing ingest lag.
- Alerting should consider telemetry lag as a separate signal (see incident 1769032199).

2) Report two rollups everywhere: request-attributable and all-in
- Console: show request-attributable by default + a toggle/tooltip for overhead/all-in.
- Finance: all-in for monthly close; request-attributable for product optimization.

3) Lock semantics in the Standard Cost Model schema (reject ambiguous inputs)
- If batch_efficiency or cache_hit_rate is missing/invalid, cost model should return explicit warnings and degrade gracefully (bounded default) rather than silently applying the wrong multiplier.

4) Build a small “drift triage playbook”
- When drift spikes:
  - Check telemetry lag dashboard
  - Check schema version distribution
  - Check for recent runtime exporter changes
  - Check untagged spend share

Next steps / owners
- Thomas: draft drift SLI definition + dashboard panels (tie into ENG-4827)
- Logan/Nadia: confirm token split conformance test approach; propose acceptance thresholds
- Mei: propose watermark/backfill policy options for daily vs monthly jobs
- Cole/Laura: align on overhead allocation knobs that must be in v1 outputs
- Rafael: incident response runbook inputs (what to do when drift alert fires but lag is the root)

Appendix A — scratch table (examples)
(Values are illustrative from sampled days; do not treat as final reporting numbers)

Date       | Region     | Observed Spend ($) | Predicted Request Attr ($) | Predicted All-in ($) | Drift (All-in)
---------- | ---------- | ------------------ | --------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------
2026-02-06 | us-east-1  | 182,400            | 171,900                     | 176,500              | -3.2%
2026-02-11 | us-east-1  | 190,100            | 206,800                     | 212,900              | +12.0%  (bug/backfill)
2026-02-14 | eu-west-1  | 96,700             | 90,200                      | 92,100               | -4.8%
2026-02-17 | dedicatedA | 44,300             | 33,800                      | 36,100               | -18.5% (idle/headroom)

Appendix B — notes to self
- If we don’t separate policy vs measurement, the project will stall in debates about “accuracy”.
- Expect Console vs Finance needs to diverge; schema should support both without hidden assumptions.
- Tie every drift chart to: (1) freshness, (2) schema version, (3) overhead policy version.
